items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

items.guide_markdown:
# Locality Guide: Rowan County, North Carolina (1839-1899)

No statewide civil death registration until 1913 — probate/estate files (1753-1970) are the primary substitute. A father's estate could be probated any time from his child's infancy to roughly 60 years after the child's birth; size the search window to the father's plausible lifespan, not the child's own.

planItems.rationale: Keyword search for the surname Voss across the Rowan County Probate Records, 1839-1899 image group (004900301, full-text searchable, about 40% name-indexed), looking for an estate, will or guardianship file that names Caroline as a daughter. The window runs from Caroline's birth year to roughly 60 years after it because a father's estate could be probated at any point in his lifetime after that, and is not capped at her circa-1858 marriage. Only the marriage record (log_001) has been searched so far. A will or estate file naming her as daughter would be direct parentage evidence.

Name search for the surname Voss in the North Carolina Estate Files, 1663-1979 collection (name-searchable, statewide), filtered to Rowan County. It runs in parallel with the county probate search so that an estate file indexed here but not in the county image group is still found. Caroline's father's estate is the target, and a file naming her as heir settles the parentage question.

Browse the Rowan County Probate Records, 1839-1899 image group (004900301, 4,120 images) by year for Voss estate files, used when the full-text search in the first item misses an entry because of OCR error, spelling variant or an unindexed page. It is the fallback for that search, not a separate source, and is needed because only about 40% of the volume is name-indexed.

Full-text co-occurrence search for Caroline and Voss together in the Rowan probate records (not a phrase search), testing for guardianship bonds, heirs lists or distribution accounts that name her as a minor heir. This is a FAN-directed item: an administrator bond or guardianship often names the children and their guardian, and it can reveal the father's estate when the father's own file is not indexed.

Browse the North Carolina Probate Records, 1735-1970 collection (browse-only) for Rowan County Voss files. It is the fallback if the Rowan County Probate Records search in the second item finds no estate file. Browse-only, so it needs image browsing rather than a name search.

Search the North Carolina Wills and Deeds collection (name-searchable) for a will of a Voss father recorded in a deed book, which is where a will was often copied when no probate file survives. This is the fallback for the first item, and it tests whether a will names Caroline as daughter.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

Locate that certificate in the name-searchable Pennsylvania Death Certificates collection (1906-1968, state registration in force) and read the father and mother fields. A 1908 certificate is a state-registered record, so its parent fields are a direct parentage test. This is the first item because it may name the parents outright.

Patrick's birth is ~1845, recorded in the tree as Ireland, while the question's objective states Pennsylvania. The tree's birth fact cites the 1850 census, not a birth or baptism record. Search the name-searchable Births and Christenings and Schuylkill County church records for a baptism naming Thomas Flynn as father. Whether a Schuylkill parish register reaches back to the 1840s is not recorded in the locality entry, and an Irish baptism would fall outside this collection set, so a negative result does not settle the birthplace question.

Parents' marriage: confirms Thomas Flynn as a married man with a wife before Patrick's birth, and if this is Thomas's first marriage, supplies the mother's maiden name, which the 1850 census does not give. Search the name-searchable Compiled Marriages and Civil Marriages collections for Thomas Flynn as groom in Schuylkill County. The couple's marriage proves they married; it does not by itself place Patrick with them. Thomas's marriage is indirect for pre-1845 Schuylkill, and the locality entry flags the pre-1811 parent-county filing, which does not affect this 1835-1845 window.

FAN item: baptisms of Thomas Flynn's other children, searched in the name-searchable Births and Christenings and Schuylkill County church records. A sibling's baptism names the same parents, so it can state the mother's name even where Patrick's own baptism is missing. Search the surname Flynn with the 1850 census's Thomas Flynn household as the anchor, and check sponsors who may be kin.

Thomas Flynn's will or administration, filed with the county Register of Wills from 1811, could name Patrick as a son. The window is sized to Thomas's own lifespan, born ~1818, not to the 1850 census year, because the estate file was created at his death, which may be decades after 1850. The probate collection is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the county's dockets for the Flynn surname, not a name search.

Post-1850 co-residence: check whether Patrick, age 15-25, still lives in Thomas Flynn's household. Census name search on Thomas and Patrick with Schuylkill as residence. The 1850 record only places Patrick in the household by position and shared surname, so a later household that repeats the pairing adds corroboration. Neither census of this pair states relationships, so this is indirect evidence.

The 1880 census is the first to record each person's relationship to the head of household, so it is the first census that can state Patrick as Thomas's son rather than infer it. Search for Patrick Flynn with a birth year near 1845 in Schuylkill County, then check whether a Thomas Flynn is head of household or in the same dwelling. A match that names Patrick as son would be direct parentage evidence.

Mortality schedules record deaths in the twelve months before each census. Searching for Thomas Flynn here tests whether he died in the decade after 1850, which would set the probate and burial searches. items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

Thomas Flynn is Irish-born, and naturalization papers can name his native county and his wife and children. Search the Pennsylvania naturalization collections by name. Subject's own marriage: the County Marriages collection is name-searchable. Search Patrick Flynn as groom in Schuylkill. Some marriage entries name the groom's father, which would be direct evidence for Thomas Flynn, and the bride's family is a FAN lead.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1870-1882

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) -- browse image-by-image.
Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

planItems.rationale: The 1880 census is the nearest enumeration to the move and is name-searchable. Tree facts: F2 places Michael in Schuylkill County in 1882 and F3 gives his occupation as Miner in 1882, but the tree records no 1875-1881 location for him. The 1880 household shows whether he was already in the county, who he lived with, his age and occupation, and his neighbours, which can point to the reason for the move. log_001 (1870 census, farmer outside Schuylkill) is the 'before' point and is not repeated. The census does not state a motive.

City and business directories for the county and its mining towns, name-searchable. log_002 found a single 1882 directory entry for Michael as miner, found incidentally. Entries from 1875 to 1881 would narrow the arrival year to a season, show whether he first appears at a colliery town or a farm, and show any boarding address that links him to a relative (tree F4 places Patrick Sheahan in the county in 1875).

Deeds and leases at the Schuylkill County Recorder of Deeds, held in image form from 1811. Source S2 in the tree cites Patrick Sheahan's 1875 purchase from James Kelly (Deed Book 42, p. 118), which shows a brother already holding county land by 1875. Search the same index for any purchase, lease or mortgage by Michael. The localities entry notes that much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than bought, so a company lease is a likely form of the record and a purchase may be absent even if he moved to work.

Family member (FAN) item for Patrick Sheahan, the one relative in the tree already documented in Schuylkill County (F4, 1875 residence; S2 deed). Church marriage and baptism records, name-searchable, that name Patrick's household and his sponsors or witnesses may name Michael as a sponsor, a witness, or a member of the same household. This is the test of whether Michael followed a brother into the county. It also identifies the parish both men used, which item 5 needs.

Fallback to item 4. Roman Catholic sacramental registers stay at the parish or diocese, not the county (localities quirk: Diocese of Philadelphia, archdiocese from 1875). If the indexed church records in item 4 do not name Michael or Patrick, the parish registers themselves are the next source. The parish must first be identified from item 4 before a request is made. Michael's own marriage or children's baptisms, if they took place in the county, would show the parish and any sponsors from his home district.

Schuylkill County newspapers and mining notices. This is the only item type that could state a reason rather than a location: colliery hiring, strikes or accidents, or a notice of a relative's death or visit. No collection for the county's papers is in the localities entry, so the repository and its availability still need confirming before any search. Do not treat a hit as evidence of motive without a second source naming Michael.

Naturalization records, name-searchable in the Pennsylvania district court collections. This item applies only if Michael was foreign-born; no birthplace for him is recorded in the tree or the log. A declaration or petition would give his arrival port and date, which bounds how long he had been in the country before the 1882 move. Plan it after item 1, which can confirm birthplace, and drop it if the 1880 census shows him born in the United States.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

The marriage must have occurred before Patrick's birth, and the 1850 and 1860 households (log_001, log_004) show Thomas as head with Patrick in the household. This is a dedicated marriage search for the candidate couple. It is name-searchable in the county marriage collections for this place (Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1775-1991, and Pennsylvania, Church Marriages, 1682-1976). A marriage that proves to be a remarriage would not give her birth name, so record any earlier marriage found.

Tracks Patrick Flynn as an adult, age about 25, and tests whether he is still in Thomas Flynn's household (1850 and 1860 placed him there, log_001 and log_004). The 1870 schedule records each person's age and birthplace, so it tests the tree's Ireland birth against the objective's Pennsylvania birth. Search Patrick Flynn b. about 1845 and Thomas Flynn b. about 1818 in Schuylkill. Name-searchable: United States, Census, 1870. Check the household for Patrick's independent household if he has left home, and note any Flynn households of similar age. Indexed name variants (Flinn, Flin, Pat) should be tried before a fallback is used.

Tracks Patrick Flynn at about age 35, and finds Thomas Flynn at about age 62 with a relationship to the head recorded for each person. Test whether Thomas is head or a dependent in Patrick's household, and whether Patrick's own household includes a wife and children who would name Patrick's parents' origins. Name-searchable: United States, Census, 1880. Search Patrick Flynn b. about 1845 and Thomas Flynn b. about 1818 in Schuylkill.

Tracks Patrick Flynn at about age 55, the last census before his 1908 death in Schuylkill (pli_005, log_005). The 1900 schedule gives each person's month and year of birth and the birthplaces of each person's father and mother, so it may name the parents' birthplaces directly. Thomas Flynn, born about 1818, may already be dead by 1900, so search Patrick's household and any households of Flynns in Schuylkill for a widowed or elderly father or any relative. Name-searchable: United States, Census, 1900. The death certificate names Thomas Flynn as father (log_005), so use this census to check that the same Patrick is the one who died in 1908.

Fan item required for a parentage question. Browse the enumeration page of Thomas Flynn's household in 1870 and in 1880, once pli_007 and pli_008 have located it. Record the Irish-born neighbours, the other Flynn households, and any boarders or in-laws. A neighbour or in-law with a Flynn tie would show the household's associates and so could corroborate the Thomas Flynn to Patrick Flynn link. Browse-only image pages are not name-searchable, so this is a page-by-page check.

Fallback for the 1870 census item if the FamilySearch index misses the household because of a transcription or name-variant problem. Search the same 1870 household with Ancestry's index, which may read the names differently. Confirm any hit against the original image on FamilySearch, since an index hit is a lead, not evidence.
Fallback for the 1880 census item if the FamilySearch index misses the household. Repeat the search on Ancestry's index with name variants. Confirm any hit against the original image on FamilySearch.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1845-1908

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

Wills and administrations from 1811, recorded in indexed books; a primary parentage source naming heirs.
The orphans' court records include marriages (since 1885), births and deaths (1893-1905) and adoptions (since 1925), besides estate dockets and distributions.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
Some naturalization and church films for the anthracite coal region are browse-only image groups (volume_search shows ~0% record-searchable) - browse image-by-image.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.

Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

items.narrative_markdown:
## Parentage of Patrick Flynn (ca. 1845–1908)

Patrick Flynn is **Probably** the son of Thomas Flynn of Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania.

### Evidence Summary

Three independent lines of evidence support this conclusion:

1. **1850 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 5, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn, age 32, born Ireland, in Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (dwelling 84, family 91). The 1850 census does not state relationships, but Patrick's position in the household and shared surname are consistent with a parent-child relationship. The informant is indeterminate but likely a household member. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

2. **1860 U.S. Census** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn, age 15, born Ireland, appears in the household of Thomas Flynn in Schuylkill County (dwelling 112, family 119). Like the 1850 census, the 1860 census does not state relationships explicitly (the relationship column was not introduced until 1880). Patrick's position in the household, shared surname, and age consistent with the 1850 enumeration support a parent-child relationship. This constitutes indirect evidence of parentage.

3. **1908 Death Certificate** (Original Source). Patrick Flynn's death certificate (no. 4521, Pennsylvania Department of Health) names "Thomas Flynn" as his father. The informant was James Brown, identified as Patrick's son-in-law. As a son-in-law reporting his father-in-law's parentage, Brown is a secondary informant for this fact — he was not a witness to Patrick's birth and is reporting what he was told. Nevertheless, this is direct evidence naming the father.

### Conflict Resolution

A birthplace conflict exists: the 1850 and 1860 censuses list Patrick's birthplace as Ireland, while the 1908 death certificate states Pennsylvania. The two census records are contemporary recordings with informants likely present in the household, while the death certificate was created 63 years after Patrick's birth by a son-in-law with no firsthand knowledge of the event. Per the GPS preponderance hierarchy, contemporary recordings by closer informants outweigh later recollections by secondary informants. Ireland is accepted as the birthplace; the death certificate entry is attributed to informant error.

### Assessment

The conclusion is rated **Probable** rather than **Proved** because: (a) both census sources (1850 and 1860) provide only indirect evidence of parentage (relationships not stated — the relationship column was not introduced until 1880), (b) the death certificate informant is secondary, and (c) research is not yet exhaustive — the 1870, 1880, and 1900 censuses have not been searched, and Thomas Flynn's probate records have not been searched. If Thomas Flynn's will names Patrick as a son, or if additional census records confirm the relationship, the conclusion would advance to **Proved**.

### Citations

1. 1850 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 84, family 91, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M432, roll 810; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 1 May 2026.
2. 1860 U.S. Census, Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania, population schedule, dwelling 112, family 119, Thomas Flynn household; NARA microfilm publication M653, roll 1141; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 2 May 2026.
3. Pennsylvania Department of Health, death certificate no. 4521 (1908), Patrick Flynn; Pennsylvania State Archives, Harrisburg; digital image, FamilySearch.org, accessed 3 May 2026.

The schedule also shows whether a wife is living in the household.

Thomas Flynn's death and burial. The tree gives him as born about 1818 in Ireland (I2), and the 1850 census shows him aged 32, so his death could fall anywhere after 1850. Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 and Pennsylvania Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950 are both name-searchable. Statewide death registration began only in 1906, so for a pre-1906 death these county and cemetery entries are the likely record. An entry may name a wife or children, and its date fixes the end of the probate window in the next item.

The localities entry names probate as a primary parentage source that lists heirs. The window runs from Thomas's probable lifespan (born about 1818), not the subject's research window. Sibling evidence (FAN). Pennsylvania, Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 is name-searchable. A baptism of a later child of Thomas Flynn in the county would name both parents, which can identify the mother's name and confirm that Patrick shares them. The search should take Thomas Flynn as father, then match the children's ages to Patrick's siblings. This is the route to the mother's name if Patrick's own early register is missing.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1838-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Probate is held by the county Register of Wills from 1811. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906, so pre-1906 vital events depend on church, cemetery, and probate records. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only.

agent_returns.text:
Created plan `pl_001` for q_001 with 13 items, all still planned. I have not started the searches: I can only write the plan, so the execution hand-back goes to search-records.

**Mode:** fresh plan (no earlier plans for q_001). The question is who the other children of Bridget Halloran and John Doyle were. The project has no tree facts beyond Bridget, John and Ellen Doyle, and no log entries are tied to this question. Three earlier finds bear on it:
- The 1900 Kearney household image records 9 children born to Bridget, 2 living (log_002).
- Bridget remarried Martin Kearney in 1879 (log_001).
- Ellen Doyle's marriage, 1865-1875, names John Doyle and Bridget Halloran as her parents (log_003).

**Plan items, in order:**
1. Census 1860, Schuylkill County (name-searchable).
2. Census 1870, Schuylkill County (name-searchable).
3. Census 1880, Schuylkill County, including the Kearney household (name-searchable).
4. Census 1900, re-reading the Kearney household listing that log_002 read only for its fertility columns.
5. Baptisms, Schuylkill County, 1856-1880, searched by mother Bridget Halloran and father John Doyle (name-searchable).
6. Fallback for item 5: browse the Schuylkill Catholic baptism registers image by image (browse-only).
7. The parents' marriage, 1855-1866, searched in the county marriage records.
8. Probate on John Doyle, 1862-1900, browsed image by image at the Schuylkill Register of Wills (browse-only).
9. Deaths, burials and cemetery records for John Doyle and any child who died young, 1856-1950 (name-searchable).
10. Schuylkill Haven funeral home obituary cards and obituaries, 1914-2007, for children who survived to 1900.
11. Naturalization of John Doyle, 1840-1900, if he was an immigrant (name-searchable).
12. Friends-and-neighbours item: witnesses and bondsmen in Ellen Doyle's 1865-1875 marriage record, and Halloran relatives.
13. Find a Grave, external, for corroboration only.

Every item names only what to search for. Any name found must be tied to a record before it counts as one of Bridget's children.

Validation returned four warnings that Schuylkill County and the Pennsylvania naturalization district are "not inside any locality this project has researched." The locality survey for Pennsylvania does cover Schuylkill County, so I read those as false alarms. Plan items 5 through 12 depend on that survey's quirks, including that Catholic registers sit with the parish or diocese and that the probate collection is browse-only.

**Hand-back:** search-records — execute pl_001 items pli_001 through pli_013 in order, with pli_006 as the fallback for pli_005. Item 13 is external and belongs to search-external-sites.

---

Here is the plan for finding the other children of Bridget Halloran and John Doyle. The plan starts with the census years 1860, 1870 and 1880 in Schuylkill County, then re-reads the 1900 census page for the two surviving children. It then looks at Catholic baptism registers, the 1855-1866 parents' marriage record, John Doyle's probate file, cemetery and death records, later obituaries, his naturalization papers, and the families of the witnesses to Ellen Doyle's marriage. A browse-only fallback and an external cemetery check come last. The next step is for the search-records agent to run these items in order.

items.rationale: Name-searchable 1860 federal census. The Doyle household (John Doyle, Bridget, and any children at home) should show the earliest children of the first marriage; the 1860 schedule names each child with age and birthplace, which tests the 9-births count from log_002. Bridget is recorded as born about 1838 in Ireland (I1), so her first marriage predates 1865 per the Ellen Doyle marriage record (log_003).

Name-searchable 1870 federal census. Enumerates the John Doyle household (if John is still alive) or Bridget as a widow with her children under age, which is where the surviving Doyle children in the family group should appear. Also tests whether John was alive in 1870, which bears on the probate item below.

Name-searchable 1880 federal census. Bridget was remarried to Martin Kearney in 1879 (log_001), so the 1880 Kearney household may list Doyle children as stepchildren, and its relationship-to-head column can state each child's relation to Bridget. Mortality-schedule deaths in the year before this census are also checked through the 1850-1880 mortality schedule collection in the cemetery and death item.

The 1900 Kearney household page was read only for its fertility columns (log_002: 9 children born, 2 living). Re-read the same page for its household listing, which names the two living children with ages and birthplaces; that listing is the only source in hand that names the surviving children directly. Name-searchable 1900 census, so the household can also be searched by Kearney and Doyle.

items.jurisdiction: Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania (Roman Catholic parishes, Diocese of Philadelphia)
items.rationale: Name-searchable Pennsylvania Births and Christenings collection. The loc_001 quirk says Catholic sacramental registers are held by the parish or diocese, not the county, so baptisms of the Doyle children are searched here by mother's name (Bridget Halloran) and father (John Doyle) across all anthracite-region parishes that appear. Each baptism would give a child's name, date and parish. Pre-1906 civil birth registration does not exist, so baptisms are the primary birth record.

Fallback for the baptism search above. loc_001 notes that some anthracite-region church films are browse-only image groups, so if the name index does not return the Doyle baptisms, browse the Schuylkill Catholic baptism registers image by image for Doyle entries with mother Bridget.

Dedicated item for the parents' marriage. The John Doyle and Bridget Halloran marriage is the only record that dates the start of the family unit and names the mother's maiden name (Halloran) in a form that bears on her first marriage. Its date bounds the earliest possible child. This marriage does not by itself prove that any given child is Bridget's; that requires the baptism or census items. Searched in the Pennsylvania County Marriages collection, with the Church Marriages collection as a check.

Probate on John Doyle, the first husband. The Pennsylvania probate collection is browse-only for this purpose (loc_001 shows zero record-searchable content), so the Schuylkill Register of Wills docket is browsed image by image. A will or administration names heirs, which would list the Doyle children directly. The window is sized to John Doyle's plausible lifespan (born about 1820-1840, died when Bridget was still in the first marriage or soon after), not to the subject's marriage.

Deaths and burials for John Doyle and any Doyle child who died young, which often gives the age and parent names that a birth record lacks. Searched in the Pennsylvania Deaths and Burials and the Pennsylvania Cemetery Records collections, name-searchable. A child who died in childhood is still a child of the family and must be counted in the 9 births (log_002).

Schuylkill Haven funeral home obituary cards and the Pennsylvania Obituaries collection, name-searchable. Any Doyle child who survived to 1900 (the 2 living in log_002) and died after 1914 would be named with parents and siblings in an obituary or funeral card. This is the route to the surviving children's later lives and to siblings they name.

items.jurisdiction: Pennsylvania (Eastern and Middle District naturalization, applied to Schuylkill County)
items.rationale: If John Doyle was an Irish immigrant, his naturalization papers name his residence and sometimes his wife and children. Name-searchable Pennsylvania Eastern District and Middle District naturalization collections. Confirm which district held Schuylkill County cases in that period before filtering on the county. Tests John Doyle's identity and residence, which the census items rely on.

FAN item. The Ellen Doyle marriage record (log_003) names her parents, and marriage records of that period often carry bondsmen or witnesses who were relatives of the bride or groom. Search the same county marriage index for those names and for the Halloran surname, and check the Doyle and Halloran witnesses. Witnesses and bondsmen may be siblings or in-laws of Bridget, and so may name Bridget's children.

External check for the Doyle family plots in Schuylkill County cemeteries, which are often listed with family members who share a stone. Use for corroboration only; any name found here must be tied to a record above before it counts as one of Bridget's children.

quirks: Danish military levy rolls (laegdsruller) begin in 1789 and enroll every male from early childhood under his father's name — each son's entry sits directly beneath the father's, making the rolls DIRECT parentage evidence for a male subject.
Danish naming is patronymic before ~1850: 'Mikkel Nielsen' means Mikkel son of Niels, so the father's given name is Niels — the patronymic alone does not identify which Niels.
Vital events are recorded in parish church books (kirkeboeger); baptism entries name both parents. Civil registration is much later.
The Stagstrup parish register is only ~3% name-indexed on FamilySearch — plan to browse the register images by year rather than rely on the index.

items.question: Who was the father of Mikkel Nielsen Blyeberg (b. 20 Aug 1779, Stagstrup Sogn, Thisted Amt, Denmark)?
items.rationale: Primary research objective. The subject's patronymic 'Nielsen' implies a father named Niels, but no father is identified in the tree and no records have been searched yet.

planItems.rationale: Mikkel's baptism in the Stagstrup parish church book (kirkebog), which names both parents. This is the most direct route to the father's given name and farm. The Stagstrup register is only about 3% name-indexed, so browse the 1779-1780 baptism pages by year rather than relying on the index. Name forms to try when browsing: Mikkel, Michael, Mickel; father Niels, with the patronymic Nielsen. Patronymics are not unique, so the entry must name the father in full, and any farm name given with him (possibly Blyeberg) should be recorded.

The Danish levy rolls (laegdsruller) began around 1788-1789 and enrolled each boy from early childhood under his father's name, so Mikkel, aged about 9 to 13 in these years, should appear directly beneath his father's entry. This is direct parentage evidence for a son. The Denmark, Military Levying Rolls (Laegdsruller), 1789-1861 collection is name-searchable for this period. Search Mikkel Nielsen and the variants above, then check the parish and farm named against the baptism.

Later levy rolls, taken at three-year intervals, carry the same family forward. They show the father's entry and any change of parish, and they may give the year the father drops off or is marked deceased. Browse the images by roll year where the name search from item 2 does not reach a later roll. Cite the Danish supplemental-number system: a move to a new parish shows as a new parish number and supplemental number. Browse-only route for the pages the index does not cover.

The candidate parents' marriage in the Stagstrup church book, dated before Mikkel's birth. It confirms the couple as a unit and supplies the mother's maiden name, which the baptism may omit. Because Mikkel was born in 1779, the marriage should be in the years before that date. Browse the marriage pages by year, since the register is only lightly indexed. The marriage alone does not prove Mikkel is their child; that link needs the baptism or a levy roll. If the mother married more than once, add her other marriages as separate searches.

FAN search. Baptisms of Mikkel's siblings and the godparents, witnesses and neighbours named in the same register. A sibling baptism naming the same father and mother confirms the family. Godparents often include the paternal uncles and grandparents, which can point to the father's given name and farm. This tests the parentage from another angle, since a single entry can be misread.

The burial of the candidate father, which gives the date he died. The question asks when the father died, so the burial is needed. A burial entry may also name his farm and age, which checks the age against a birth around 1740-1755. Browse the burial pages by year from 1779 forward.

Mikkel's own death or burial entry. The tree holds no death date for him, so this is not yet known to have occurred. The entry may state his father's name and his age, which can confirm the father when the baptism is illegible. Browse the Stagstrup burial pages by year over the later period.

Full-text co-occurrence search for the farm name Blyeberg together with Niels, run across the church books of the area. The farm name is a place-based surname and is unlikely to be indexed as a name. It may appear in the transcribed text of baptism, marriage or burial entries, and it could link the father to a specific farm in Stagstrup or a neighbouring parish. Search the two terms as separate words, not as the compound name.

## Locality Guide: Trysil, Hedmark, Norway (1780–1880)

### Jurisdictional Context

Trysil became its own *prestegjeld* in 1780, separated from Elverum. The 1860 death falls squarely within Trysil's own records. Administratively: Amt of Hedmark from 1781; Sorenskriveri of Søndre Østerdalen; Diocese of Oslo/Christiania 1537–1864, then Hamar.

### Church Records — Primary Source

- **Digitized images** (browse-only, 0% name-indexed): Kirkebøker 1588–1928 (Trysil prestegjeld) at FamilySearch Catalog (cat. 737) and Digitalarkivet. The 1860 burial will be in volume 008679203_003 (1814–1877, 325 images).
- **Indexed national extracts** (name-searchable): Norway Burials 1666–1927 (FS col 1468081; also Ancestry, MyHeritage); Norway Baptisms 1634–1927 (FS col 1467014); Norway Marriages 1660–1926 (FS col 1468080).
- **Dissenter church**: Trysil Frimenighet 1858–1920 at Digitalarkivet (images).

### Census

| Year | FS Collection | Access | Notes |
|------|--------------|--------|-------|
| 1801 | 3733603 | indexed & images | Subject ~21; also Ancestry, MyHeritage |
| 1865 | 3756102 | indexed & images | Postdates death; shows widow/children |
| 1870 | 4135961 | indexed & images | Postdates death |
| 1875 | 1529106 | indexed & images | Postdates death; also Ancestry, MyHeritage |

### Probate

- Norway Probate Index Cards 1640–1903 (FS col 1661306): indexed — locate the 1860 estate filing here.
- Skifteprotokoller image volumes at FS Catalog cover through 1853; post-1853 volumes held at Riksarkivet/Digitalarkivet.

### Land Records

- Pantebøker (mortgage/property) 1712–1860 (FS Catalog 489152) — images.

### Military / Levy Rolls

Norway's conscription/levy rolls (*lægdsruller*) began 1789. Each enrolled boy is listed under his father's name — direct parentage evidence. A male born ~1780 would appear from approximately 1789. Access via Riksarkivet and Digitalarkivet.

### Farm Books (*Bygdebøker*)

Trysilboka (Lillevold, Larsen, Bryn; FS Library 948.23/T2 D2l) — multiple volumes covering farm histories and resident genealogies for Trysil with personal name indexes in volumes 1–3, 7–8. High-value source for locating a household at the farm level.

### Key Access Points

- **FamilySearch** (free): indexed burials/baptisms/marriages/census, browse church record images
- **Digitalarkivet** (free): church books at media.digitalarkivet.no/en/kb/browse
- **Ancestry** (subscription): Norway Burials/Baptisms/Marriages extracts, 1865 census
- **MyHeritage** (subscription): Norway Burials/Marriages, 1865/1875 census
- **FamilySearch Library** (on-site or center): Trysilboka farm book, catalog microfilm

**Ecclesiastical jurisdiction:** Kongsberg prestegjeld, Kongsberg prosti, Oslo bispedømme (until 1948). Civil jurisdiction in 1780: Buskerud amt (from 1680), Numedal og Sandsvær sorenskriveri, Kongsberg Byfogderi (probate/skifterett).

### Church Records

All Kongsberg church record volumes at FamilySearch are **browse-only** (0% name-indexed, not full-text searchable). Browse image by image.

- Same extracts also at Ancestry (Norway Select Baptisms col 60092) and MyHeritage

**Digitalarkivet:** Complete parish register scans 1696–1969 at media.digitalarkivet.no (Buskerud county, Kongsberg prestegjeld). Both Kongsberg proper and Jondalen sub-parish registers are available. Same material as FS volumes; browse by year range.

### Census Records

Norwegian levy rolls began 1789. A male born ~1780 enrolled ~age 7–9, listed directly **under his father's name** — direct parentage evidence. Access: Digitalarkivet (browse and search) and Riksarkivet physical holdings for Numedal og Sandsvær lægd.

### Probate Records
- Kongsberg Byfogderi Skifteprotokoller 1739–1851 (FS Catalog 437559, browse-only; also Digitalarkivet)
- Norway Probate Index Cards 1640–1903 (FS col 1661306, indexed)

Search Hoval Hansen with variants Haaval Hansen, Havald, Håval Ziener and Ziener, and read each hit's godparents and parents. Per loc_002, the 1780s coverage of this extract may be incomplete, so a nil result is a reason to go to item 3, not a conclusion.

The subject's own burial entry for 18 August 1860. Norway burial registers of this era routinely state age and home parish or birthplace, which is the bridge back to the Kongsberg baptism if the baptism cannot be found directly. The Norway Burials 1666-1927 extract (collection 1468081) is name-searchable. Trysil was its own clerical district from 1780 (loc_001), so the entry sits in Trysil and not Elverum. Search Hoval, Haaval, Håval Hansen and Ziener.

Browse of the prime Kongsberg baptism register for a c.1780 birth (volume 008680156_003, 1769-1782), which is browse-only and must be read image by image for the entry. This is the fallback for item 1 when the name index returns nothing or misses the 1780s. It is the primary source the index extract is drawn from, so it is the verification step for any index hit (Standard 13). Record the godparents, the father's name and the mother's name from the entry.

Browse of the Trysil church record volume 008679203_003 (1814-1877), which is browse-only and must be read image by image to find the 18 August 1860 burial entry. This is the fallback for item 2 if the name index does not return the entry. The entry may state the subject's age and home parish or birthplace, which would point the baptism search to the right parish.

The same Norway baptism extracts appear on Ancestry (Norway Select Baptisms). The subscription is in the project's list, so this is a second name-searchable route to the item 1 extract with its own search engine and transcription. It is a paid fallback for item 1, searched only after the FamilySearch index is exhausted, and any hit must still be checked against the register image (item 3).

Wider-window browse if the 1769-1782 register does not carry the entry. Volume 008680157_002 (1783-1797, browse-only) covers the years after a c.1780 birth where a late or delayed baptism is possible, and the later register runs into the 1790s. It is the fallback for item 3.

Dedicated search for the parents' marriage, separate from the baptism. The Norway Marriages 1660-1926 extract (collection 1468080) is name-searchable. The father is not yet known, so search the surname Ziener and the candidate surname Hansen for Kongsberg marriages in the years before a c.1780 birth. The marriage supplies the mother's maiden name if it was her first marriage, and its date relative to the birth corroborates a parent. It does not by itself prove the subject is their child. Hold the surname as a search key only, not a finding: Ziener may be a later or alternate name.

The 1801 census (collection 3733603) is name-searchable and is the first household record that can place a man of about 21 with his parents. It is the only census before 1865 in the locality set, and it may show the subject in a father's household, which is direct parentage evidence. Read the household members and their stated ages. The census does not give birthplace, so it corroborates rather than proves parentage. Search Kongsberg and also Trysil, since the family may have moved between 1780 and 1801.

Levy rolls (lægdsruller), which began in 1789 for this jurisdiction. A boy born about 1780 is enrolled from about age 7 to 9 under his father's name, so a roll naming him beside a father is direct parentage evidence where the baptism register is unreadable. Source for this rule is the locality guide (loc_002), not the Norway Military Records wiki page, which does not describe the rolls. Access is Digitalarkivet for browse and search, and Riksarkivet for physical holdings. Read the roll for the district and farm, then check it against items 1 and 8.

The Trysilboka farm book (FS Library 948.23/T2 D2l, several volumes) gives farm-level residents and genealogies for Trysil, with personal name indexes in volumes 1-3 and 7-8. This is the FAN item for the question: it covers the farm households, neighbours and any sibling of the subject, and it may name a Ziener or Hansen household whose children include him. Check the name indexes first for Ziener and Hansen, then the farm entries. It is a lead source (Standard 13), so each entry is checked against a record before it is used.

The Norway Probate Index Cards (collection 1661306) are name-searchable and locate the estate of the subject, who died 18 August 1860. An estate filing can name his heirs, including siblings and a surviving spouse or child, and so gives FAN names. The index card gives the reference only. The actual volume must then be retrieved from Riksarkivet or Digitalarkivet, since the FamilySearch skifte volumes run only to 1853 (loc_001).

items.guide_markdown:
## Guadalajara, Jalisco, Mexico - 1880-1920

Although Mexicans use two surnames, most indexed records carry only the first (paternal) surname — search with the paternal surname alone; when the person is not found, search through the parents (a parent search with each parent's first surname, leaving out the child's name). quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.

planItems.rationale: Patrick Flynn's own death, 1908-03-12 in Schuylkill County (tree fact F2, cited to S3, Pennsylvania Death Certificates). Pennsylvania statewide certificates from 1906 usually name the decedent's father and mother, so this is the most direct route to the parents. The tree records the death place and date only, not the parents' names, so the parents' names are unread. Index search on Pennsylvania, Deaths and Burials, 1720-1999 (name-searchable) for the entry, then read the certificate itself.

Fallback for item 1: if the indexed entry does not show the parents, obtain the state death certificate for Patrick Flynn, died 1908, Schuylkill County, from the Department of Health. Access route unknown in the locality entry; confirm before relying on it.

Thomas Flynn household, the head of the 1850 household that held Patrick age 5 (log_001, dwelling 84). The 1860 census (name-searchable, United States Census 1860) has not been searched, and it is the gap between 1851 and 1860 in the timeline (t_001). It may name Thomas's wife and show whether Patrick still lives with his father, and it is already cited as S2 in the tree but unread.

Re-read of the full 1850 household of Thomas Flynn (dwelling 84, family 91) and the adjoining dwellings 83 and 85. The earlier search (log_001) extracted only Patrick, so the wife's name and any siblings are unrecorded. The 1850 census names only the head of household by relationship and gives no mother's name explicitly, so the wife's name and the children's ages are the leads here. Neighbouring Flynn or Irish-born households are FAN leads (BCG Standard 14) for kin.

Marriage of the candidate parents, Thomas Flynn (b. ~1818, Ireland, tree fact F3) and his wife. This is the parents' marriage record: it supplies the mother's maiden name if this was her first marriage, and by its date relative to Patrick's birth it corroborates Thomas as father. It does not by itself prove Patrick is their child. Searched in Pennsylvania, County Marriages, 1775-1991 (name-searchable). The marriage may have taken place in Ireland, so a negative result here does not end the search.

Fallback for item 5: the same parents' marriage in the church register, Pennsylvania, Church Marriages, 1682-1976 (name-searchable). Catholic sacramental registers for Schuylkill were kept by the Diocese of Philadelphia and the parishes, not the county, so this is the register most likely to name the couple's parish.

Companion test for item 5: Thomas Flynn's wife may have married before, so the surname she gives may not be her birth name. Search Thomas Flynn's marriages and any earlier marriage of his wife in County Marriages, 1775-1991, to learn whether the 1850 household belongs to a first or later marriage. Under the wife's name the marriage record gives the maiden name only if it was her first marriage.

Probate of Thomas Flynn, if he died in the county after 1850. Wills and administrations from 1811 name heirs, which can name sons and a wife. The date range is sized to Thomas's own lifespan (born ca. 1818, so death plausibly to ca. 1905), not to the 1850 census. Pennsylvania Probate Records, 1683-1994 is browse-only, so this is an image browse of the Register of Wills index, not a name search.

Burial of Thomas Flynn, or of his wife, in a Schuylkill cemetery, in Pennsylvania, Cemetery Records, ca. 1700-ca. 1950 (name-searchable). Burial entries often state age or birth year, which tests Thomas's identity and dates the family. They rarely name parents, so this corroborates rather than establishes parentage.

FAN search for Patrick's siblings: baptisms of other children of Thomas Flynn in Pennsylvania, Births and Christenings, 1709-1950 (name-searchable). ## Västra Karaby, Malmöhus, Sweden — 1675-1750

The parish of the 1712 marriage. Its birth register begins in 1688, so a birth in the 1680s may predate it. The registers are browse-only on FamilySearch.

planItems.rationale: Elena's own marriage to Jöns Jönsson on 29 December 1712 (tree fact F3, Västra Karaby). A marriage entry often names the bride's father, her home parish or her birth parish, and it is the first record to read because it is known to exist. Marriage register image group 004523018 is 0% name-indexed; browse by year. Its parish is loc_002, whose birth register begins in 1688, so the 1712 marriage entry is inside the register.

Elena's baptism, to fix her birth and name both parents. Her marriage in 1712 and child in 1718 put her birth roughly 1680-1692. loc_002 says the Västra Karaby birth and baptism register begins in 1688, so a birth before 1688 has no entry here. Search the Sweden Baptisms index (1520594, name-searchable) for Elena with a father named Asmund, then browse image groups 004523018 and 004523021 by year, since both are 0% indexed.

The marriage of Elena's parents, Asmund and his wife, which confirms the couple as a unit and gives the mother's name. The surname Asmundsdotter is a patronymic from the father's given name Asmund (Sweden_Naming_Customs), so it does not identify which Asmund. The marriage may fall before the 1688 register start in loc_002, and then the Sweden Marriages index (1520596) and neighbouring parishes will be needed. Plan for both: search the index first, then browse image group 004523021 (1662-1850).

Burial of Elena's father Asmund, or of her mother, dated after the children were born. A burial entry often gives the deceased's age and the surviving widow's name. The window is sized to a father of a child born 1680-1692, who could have died anywhere from then to about 1730. Search the Sweden Burials index (1520597), then browse image group 004523018.

Full-text co-occurrence search for the names Elena and Asmund (both required as separate terms), run across the Västra Karaby register volumes. The volumes are 0% name-indexed (image groups 004523021 and 004523018), so an indexed search on Elena will not find her in her parents' entries. This is the fallback if the baptism item fails to name her parents.

FAN item: baptisms of Elena's siblings, which name the same parents and so would confirm Elena's family as a unit. Also check godparents, who are often kin. Browse image group 004523021 (1687-1729 coverage row) and 004523018 by year, since neither is indexed.

Household tax lists (mantalslängder) for the härad survive from 1658 and name the members of each household. A list placing Asmund's household in Västra Karaby with a daughter Elena would connect her to the parents without relying on the surname. The lists are held by Riksarkivet, not FamilySearch, so this is an access-route check, not an online search.

Elena's own death or burial entry in Barsebäck, the parish where she lived with Jöns after 1712. Such an entry often gives her age and birthplace, which the baptism may not, since the birth may predate the Västra Karaby register (loc_002). Barsebäck registers reach back to 1648 (loc_001), but they are 0% name-indexed; browse image groups 004514823 and 004514824 by year.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright by laborers.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead.

items.guide_markdown:
## Schuylkill County, Pennsylvania - 1840-1900

Schuylkill County (formed 1811 from Berks and Northampton) lies in Pennsylvania's anthracite coal region. Deed/land records are held by the county Recorder of Deeds from 1811; much coal-region land was leased from mining companies rather than purchased outright. Catholic parishes stayed with the Diocese (from 1875 the Archdiocese) of Philadelphia until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961. Statewide civil vital registration began only in 1906 -- pre-1906 events are recorded in church, cemetery, and probate records instead. Some coal-region naturalization and church films are browse-only. Curated external links reach county tax and exoneration lists for 1768-1801 only, before this period.

quirks: Schuylkill County was formed in 1811 from Berks and Northampton counties; pre-1811 records are filed under the parent counties.
Probate records (wills, administrations) are held by the county Register of Wills, available from 1811 - a primary parentage source naming heirs.

Roman Catholic parishes stayed under the Diocese of Philadelphia (an archdiocese from 1875) until the Diocese of Allentown was erected in 1961; the Diocese of Scranton, erected in 1868, took the northern counties, not Schuylkill. Sacramental registers are held at the parish/diocese, not the county.
Pennsylvania statewide civil birth/death registration did not begin until 1906; a 1908 death has a state certificate, but pre-1906 events rely on church, cemetery, and probate records.
